svg.title: The five steps that build a link-state database, and the three design corollaries
svg.desc: Five boxes in sequence. Step one: neighbour discovery and adjacency, which requires Hello and dead intervals, area, authentication and MTU to match. Step two: exchange link state advertisements, each router describing who it is connected to and at what cost. Step three: cost is carried inside the advertisement, so the meaning of the metric must be identical network-wide. Step four: every router in the area must hold exactly the same database. Step five: run Dijkstra rooted at self to build the shortest path tree. Under the sequence, three corollaries: database consistency is a hard requirement because inconsistent databases mean different topologies and possible loops; the size of the flooding domain drives convergence time and memory, because every change floods everywhere and everyone recomputes; and the metric is the only path knob available apart from areas and summarization.

The design reading: steps 1–4 are the price you pay for step 5. You are not buying shortest paths — you already
knew the shortest path. You are buying the guarantee that every router computes the same one from the same evidence.
Consequence for the design document: the flooding domain is a quantity to be sized, not a topology accident. It is sized by the area split,
and the area split is sized by the addressing plan — which is why step 1 of the methodology comes before step 2.
